reports.title: The Strait Nobody Can Open
reports.subtitle: The Hormuz blockade is costing $2 billion a day in global shipping, yet neither side can afford the deal that would end it.

reports.title: Powell's Last Days
reports.subtitle: The Fed chair's departure is essentially priced in at 95%. What comes next is the part that matters.

reports.title: Britain's Party System Is Breaking
reports.subtitle: Reform UK is the biggest winner in the local elections. The real winner is a political system that cannot handle what British voters now want.

reports.title: The Summit That Has to Look Like Nothing
reports.subtitle: Trump and Xi have more to gain from a deal than from a standoff. The problem is neither can afford to say so.

reports.title: The Permanent Gerrymander
reports.subtitle: After the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act, Republicans are redrawing maps without legal constraint. Democrats are about to learn what structural disadvantage really feels like.

reports.title: The Price of Playing Both Sides
reports.subtitle: Pakistan tried to mediate between the US and Iran. The UAE responded by expelling hundreds of thousands of Pakistani workers. That is what it costs to be indispensable.

reports.title: After Orban
reports.subtitle: Peter Magyar just became Hungary's prime minister. His hardest problem isn't Orban's loyalists. It's the system Orban built to survive anyone who tried to replace him.

reports.title: Putin Says the War Is Ending. He Means Something Different by That.
reports.subtitle: A three-day ceasefire, North Korean troops on Red Square, and Putin telling reporters the matter is 'coming to an end' — none of this means what it sounds like.

reports.title: One Year After Operation Sindoor: Both Sides Won, Neither Side Is Safer
reports.subtitle: India and Pakistan each claim victory in last May's four-day aerial war. The mutual claim of victory is not spin — it is the most dangerous thing about the ceasefire that ended it.

reports.title: Apple Just Ended ChatGPT's Exclusive Status. OpenAI Should Be Worried.
reports.subtitle: iOS 27 will let users choose Claude, Gemini, or any approved AI to power Siri. Apple is not becoming an AI company. It is becoming the platform every AI company must pay to reach.

reports.title: The Administration Has Defied Courts 31 Times. Nobody Has Stopped It.
reports.subtitle: A new review finds the Trump administration has violated federal court orders at least 31 times. The question is no longer whether the rule of law is being broken. It is whether anyone with the power to enforce it will.

reports.title: The Trump-Xi Summit Is About Iran. China Wants It That Way.
reports.subtitle: The US-China summit next week was supposed to be about tariffs and rare earths. Iran has displaced both topics. That displacement is not accidental — it is the best outcome China could have engineered.

reports.title: Iran Rejected the US Proposal. Trump Called It Unacceptable. Now What?
reports.subtitle: Tehran's counteroffer focused on ending the war. Washington's proposal required ending the nuclear program first. Those are not the same negotiation.

reports.title: Trump Got His Fed Chair. He May Get Rate Hikes.
reports.subtitle: Kevin Warsh spent a year promising he would cut rates. Then the Iran war made that impossible. Now the only question is how high rates go.

reports.title: The Stablecoin Bill Is Four Days From a Vote. Banks Just Tried to Kill It.
reports.subtitle: The CLARITY Act cleared the House with 294 votes. Banks rejected the Senate compromise the weekend before the markup. The argument is about yield. The war is about deposits.

reports.title: New Mexico Wants to Redesign Instagram. Meta Says It Will Leave the State First.
reports.subtitle: A judge who calls himself a reluctant legislator must now decide whether a state AG can force a global platform to change its algorithm. The answer will determine whether courts can regulate what Congress won't.

reports.title: The EU Spent Three Years Writing the World's Toughest AI Law. Then It Rewrote It.
reports.subtitle: The AI Act Omnibus delays most high-risk rules to 2027 and 2028. The Digital Omnibus, the sequel, may gut the data protection framework that makes AI development in Europe structurally different from China and the US.
